lesson.title: When Numbers Actually Mean Something: Quantitative Variables
lesson.summary: This section defines quantitative variables as those whose values are true numeric measurements that support meaningful arithmetic, contrasts them with categorical variables, and works through averaging the classroom quiz scores.
lesson.body:
A quantitative variable, sometimes called a numeric variable, is a variable whose recorded values are genuine measurements or counts, meaning arithmetic performed on them produces a meaningful result. This is the key test that separates a quantitative variable from a categorical one, discussed in the previous section. If it makes sense to add two values together, subtract them, or average a whole column of them, and the result means something real about the individuals being studied, the variable is quantitative. Height, weight, age, temperature, price, and quiz score are all quantitative for exactly this reason: an average height of 62 inches is a meaningful, interpretable number.

Quantitative variables always come with units, whether those units are inches, dollars, seconds, or simple counts like "number of siblings." The unit is part of what makes the arithmetic meaningful. Saying a student is 62 inches tall means something specific and comparable to another student's height in the same units. This is a further contrast with categorical variables, whose values are names with no unit attached at all. There is no unit for "brown," but there is a unit, inches, for every recorded height.

Having a unit also means that differences between quantitative values carry real meaning, not just the values themselves. If one student is 66 inches tall and another is 59 inches tall, subtracting gives a difference of 66 minus 59, which equals 7 inches, and that 7 inches genuinely describes how much taller the first student is. Try the same subtraction with a categorical variable and it falls apart instantly. There is no meaningful way to "subtract" the category male from the category female, because categories are names, not points on a numeric scale. This ability to add, subtract, and average in a way that produces answers you can actually interpret is the defining feature of a quantitative variable, and it is the reason quantitative data supports a much wider range of statistical tools than categorical data does.

Return to the classroom dataset's quiz score column: 7, 8, 6, 9, 7, 5, 8, 10 points, one score per student out of a possible 10 points. Because quiz score is quantitative, it is entirely reasonable to compute its average. Adding the 8 scores gives 7 + 8 + 6 + 9 + 7 + 5 + 8 + 10 = 60. Dividing that sum by the number of students, 8, gives an average quiz score of 60 divided by 8, which equals exactly 7.5 points. That average, 7.5, is a single number that meaningfully summarizes the typical performance of the whole class, and it is only possible to compute because quiz score is a real numeric measurement rather than a category label. It would be nonsensical to try to average the categorical gender values from the previous section the same way.

Quantitative variables can be further split into two subtypes based on what kinds of numeric values they can actually take. Some quantitative variables can only take specific separated values, usually whole numbers you get by counting, like the number of siblings a student has. Others can take any value within a range, limited only by how precisely you can measure, like height or weight. The next two sections examine these subtypes in detail: discrete variables, which are countable, and continuous variables, which are measurable along an unbroken scale. Recognizing which subtype a quantitative variable belongs to affects exactly how its distribution should be graphed and described later in this course.
